content: A crisis hotline is a dedicated telephone service that individuals can contact to receive immediate, real-time counseling during emergencies. These services are typically staffed by trained volunteers who provide support and guidance over the phone. Crisis hotlines have been operational in most major cities across the United States since at least the mid-1970s. Initially, their primary purpose was to assist individuals contemplating suicide. Over time, many of these hotlines expanded their scope to address a broader range of emotional crises. In addition to suicide prevention, similar hotlines have been established to support individuals in other challenging situations, such as survivors of sexual assault, runaway children, and members of the LGBTQ+ community, including those who identify as gay, lesbian, bisexual, transgender, or intersex. The concept of crisis hotlines dates back to 1953, when Chad Varah, an English vicar, founded The Samaritans service in the United Kingdom. This organization quickly grew, establishing branches throughout the UK. In the United States, the San Francisco Suicide Prevention organization launched a hotline called Call Bruce in 1962. Similarly, in Australia, a service known as Lifeline was established in 1963. In 1968, concerned citizens in Launceston, Tasmania, founded Lifelink Samaritans, a completely volunteer-run crisis hotline. This service provides 24-hour emotional support to callers across Tasmania and operates without any religious affiliations. Lifelink Samaritans is a member of Befrienders Worldwide and maintains a twinning relationship with Northampton Samaritans in the UK. It is the oldest telephone befriending service in Tasmania and the fourth oldest in Australia. Historically, suicide hotlines faced criticism for their perceived limitations. It was argued that individuals who were resolute in their decision to end their lives were unlikely to reach out for help. Additionally, those experiencing social anxiety might lack the emotional capacity to make such a call. Until recently, there was no concrete evidence to suggest that the existence of suicide hotlines reduced suicide rates. However, a 2007 study disproved this notion. The study demonstrated that individuals' suicidal thoughts decreased during a call to a crisis hotline and remained reduced for several weeks following the call.
